summary: Gives an initial list of requirements for IP over ATM networks, prepared by the IETF IP over ATM Working Group for the ATM Forum's Multiprotocol BOF. It is informational.

eli5.summary: The internet group tells the ATM group what it needs for the two networks to work together.

questions: how does ip work over atm
what is the classical ip over atm model
how should atm handle internet traffic
subtitle: IETF recommendations for the ATM Forum's work on connecting IP networks with ATM.

tldr.problem: The ATM Forum and the IETF needed to coordinate on how IP networks would work over ATM infrastructure. The IETF IP over ATM Working Group needed to communicate its requirements formally to the ATM Forum.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC documents the IETF's initial list of requirements for IP over ATM networks, covering standardization process, encapsulation, routing, security, multicast, addressing and quality of service, to guide the ATM Forum's Multiprotocol working group.
tldr.outcome: The document served as input to the ATM Forum, helping shape multiprotocol support in ATM networks. Over time, the IP over ATM standards evolved through multiple RFCs and vendor implementations.

today: RFC 1754 is Informational and has not been updated or obsoleted. The IETF and ATM Forum continued to collaborate on IP over ATM standards, with subsequent RFCs refining the approach. As IP and Ethernet technology evolved, ATM's role in the network infrastructure declined, though the coordination principles established here remain relevant for cross-standards-body collaboration.

sections.title: Background and Purpose
sections.content:
In the mid-1990s, Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) was seen as a promising technology for high-speed networking, and both the IETF and the ATM Forum (an industry consortium) were working on how to run IP over ATM networks. Many IETF participants worked at companies that were also principal members of the ATM Forum, but communication between the two organizations had been informal.

In July 1994, the ATM Forum Liaison formally requested that the IETF's IP over ATM Working Group prepare a list of requirements as input to the ATM Forum's Multiprotocol BOF (Birds of a Feather) activities. This RFC is the response to that request, documenting the IETF's initial requirements for supporting IP over ATM networks.

The document emphasizes that IETF standards define how the TCP/IP protocol suite is deployed over specific network technologies, and that any changes affecting those standards must be made through the public IETF standards process.
sections.eli5: Two big groups—one for the Internet and one for ATM phone cables—needed to talk about how to make them work together. This memo is what the Internet group asked for.

sections.title: Core Encapsulation and Routing Requirements
sections.content:
The IETF required that any ATM Forum work support RFC 1483 (Multiprotocol Encapsulation over ATM Adaptation Layer 5) and RFC 1577 (Classical IP and ARP over ATM) as specified. These RFCs defined how IP packets are encapsulated and carried over ATM networks. Any future changes to these standards would have to go through the IETF standards process, not be decided by ATM Forum alone.

For routing, the RFC 1577 Logical IP Subnet (LIS) model defines the default behavior. The IETF was also developing the Next Hop Resolution Protocol (NHRP) in the Routing over Large Clouds Working Group, which would allow incremental optimization of routing by using preferred ATM paths.

The IETF made one operational request: ATM signaling should indicate whether a connection is over a LAN or WAN and provide feedback on time-based versus byte-based charging, so that end systems could make informed decisions about routing.
sections.eli5: Use these specific ways to wrap up Internet packets in ATM format, don't change them without asking the Internet group, and tell us if you're charging by time or by how much data goes through.

sections.title: Security, Multicast, and Addressing
sections.content:
For security, the IETF requested that ATM signaling support a user information element to convey security and authentication information between IP members and applications, with the IETF defining the IP-specific content of this element.

For broadcast and multicast, the IETF was still discussing how to map IP multicast facilities onto ATM facilities. However, the IETF supported the ATM Forum's planned multicast enhancements such as leaf-initiated joins and multiple multicast congestion management policies.

For addressing and signaling, the IETF was producing a specification for UNI 3.0 and 3.1 signaling to support the core encapsulation RFCs. Regarding IPv6 (then called IPng), the IETF noted that IPv6 packets would include a Flow ID field intended to support service classes, and that there would likely be a mapping between IPv6 addresses and NSAP (OSI) addresses within the 20-byte NSAP format.
sections.eli5: Let IP add its own security tags, figure out how to do group messaging, and help IPv6 connect to ATM's address system.

sections.title: Quality of Service and Performance
sections.content:
The IETF laid out expectations for how ATM should handle Internet traffic. ATM should efficiently support bursty, elastic applications (those whose bandwidth varies over time). For elastic applications as defined in RFC 1633, ATM should achieve high bottleneck utilization while keeping delay reasonably bounded, without compromising delay-sensitive service classes.

ATM should provide a service class that cooperates with the TCP congestion avoidance algorithm, supporting not only directly ATM-attached systems but also traditional LAN-attached systems using current TCP implementations interconnected via ATM-attached bridges and routers.

The IETF requested both predictive QoS (for applications tolerant of delay variation and low loss) and guaranteed QoS. Since IP uses both point-to-point and multipoint connections, an ABR-like (Available Bit Rate) service would need to apply to both types. The IETF emphasized that specifications should be as simple as possible, provide full line-rate transmission over idle links, and achieve cell loss on the order of 3 in 10^8 cells for 1500-byte frames under typical conditions.
sections.eli5: Handle both steady and bursty traffic fairly, work well with how the Internet learns to send data, and keep delays predictable for real-time uses.
